body.x: Most people first hear the word khula at the worst moment of their lives, when a marriage has already broken down and a wife knows she cannot remain in it. This article explains, calmly and in general terms, what khula is in the Shia (Twelver) tradition, how it differs from the other forms of separation, and how the process ordinarily unfolds. It is information, not a ruling: every real case belongs in front of a qualified scholar, and nothing here replaces one.

Khula is a form of divorce that begins with the wife. Its defining feature is her deep aversion — a settled inability to continue the marriage — together with an offer of compensation, often called the fidya, to the husband in return for her release. In its classical shape, that compensation is the return of her mehr, or part of it, or another agreed sum or property. The marriage is then dissolved through the formal divorce formula, and the separation is irrevocable: unlike an ordinary revocable divorce, the husband cannot simply take her back during her waiting period. If, during that period, she withdraws the compensation she gave, the legal position can change — one of several details a scholar must handle in the individual case.
Khula, talaq and mubarat: the difference

Talaq is the husband-initiated divorce: he, or his appointed representative, pronounces the formula, no compensation changes hands, and in its revocable form he may take his wife back during her iddah. Khula reverses the initiative: it is her request and her compensation that set it in motion, although the formula itself is still pronounced on the husband's side. Mubarat sits between the two: there, the aversion is mutual — both spouses wish to part — and the compensation, by the well-known rule, must not exceed the mehr. Families sometimes use these words loosely; scholars do not, because the conditions and consequences of each route differ.
Details vary between marja offices and between countries, but a khula handled properly generally moves through the same stages:

Consultation: the wife, often with a parent or trusted elder, speaks to a scholar or her marja's office, which first establishes the facts — is the marriage religiously valid and ongoing, has a civil divorce been filed, is there coercion, abuse or danger?
Space for repair: where there is any safe possibility, the scholar will usually encourage mediation or counselling first. Where there is harm, or a settled and genuine aversion, the process is not blocked by endless delay.
Agreement on the compensation: what she will return or give, and its amount, is settled explicitly and recorded.
The formula (sigha): the divorce is pronounced in the required Arabic form by the husband or his appointed representative, in the presence of two upright male witnesses, and subject to conditions the scholar verifies, including those concerning her menstrual state.
Documentation: the office records the divorce, its date and its type, and issues written confirmation, which she will need for any future marriage and for her civil paperwork.

If a husband refuses to cooperate at all, the case does not simply die. In Twelver practice the religious authority — the hakim al-shar', in modern terms a marja's office or its appointed representative — can examine the case and, where the legal conditions are met, require the separation to be carried out. How that power is exercised differs between marjas, which is precisely why the route runs through an office and not through family pressure.

A woman divorced by khula observes an iddah, a waiting period, before she may marry again. In its general established form it matches the iddah of divorce: three menstrual cycles for a woman who menstruates, three months for one who does not but is of an age where she might, and until the birth if she is pregnant. During the iddah of a khula she is not maintained by her former husband in the way a revocably divorced wife is, and the marriage cannot be resumed unless she withdraws her compensation — again, a point for the scholar handling the case. When the iddah ends, she is free to marry, and a khula in her history is a fact of her past, not a stain on her character.
The civil divorce runs on a separate track

In Britain, North America, Australia and most of the diaspora, a religious divorce — khula included — does not by itself dissolve a civil marriage, and a civil divorce does not by itself end the religious one. Both tracks usually have to be completed, in whichever order the situation allows: she may need her religious divorce certificate for a future nikah and her civil decree for everything else. Courts in some countries will ask about a religious divorce where one party is accused of withholding it, but the law differs by jurisdiction, so take local legal advice alongside religious guidance, especially where children, property or immigration status are involved.

Finally, the part no form can hold. A woman seeking khula is usually doing so after a long private struggle, and the tradition that gives her this route also commands that she be treated with dignity inside it — no public shaming, no ransom demands dressed up as compensation, no family verdicts delivered over her head. If you are reading this in that position: speak to a scholar you trust, take legal advice, lean on the people who have stood by you — and if there is any question of safety, contact local support services first. The process exists so that an ending, when it must come, is lawful, documented and humane.

excerpt: Khula is the wife-initiated route out of a marriage that has become unbearable to her — a defined process in Shia law, handled through scholars, and distinct from both talaq and mubarat.
title: Khula in Shia Islam: the process explained
